title: Observing the Mind While Reciting the Buddha's Name
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Observing-the-mind recitation means that while reciting the Buddha's name, one contemplates the present single thought (reciting and contemplating at once). It is a most incisive and wondrous method, able to achieve steadily: the moment the Buddha's name is raised, all deluded thoughts vanish.

inline.s: Observing-the-mind recitation (guanxin nianfo) means that while reciting the Buddha's name, one contemplates the present single thought (reciting and contemplating at once). This is a most incisive and wondrous method, able to achieve steadily:
the moment the Buddha's name is raised, all deluded thoughts vanish.
In the course of practicing
investigative recitation
, in the stage of “all thoughts converging into one,” once you have laid a certain foundation in the investigation
, you may turn to practicing observing-the-mind recitation.

There are two ways of observing the mind while reciting: first, intermittent recitation — recite one repetition of the Buddha's name, then pause a while and closely observe the present single thought; second, continuous recitation — reciting and observing at the same time. These two ways may be applied flexibly according to the depth of one's practice and one's circumstances.
When first beginning to practice observing-the-mind recitation, you may tire easily; you may intersperse it with investigative recitation,

and then gradually shift over to observing-the-mind recitation alone. If, while practicing observing-the-mind recitation, you experience dizziness or other discomfort, it means your power of awareness is not yet sufficient; you should continue practicing investigative recitation, and only begin observing-the-mind recitation when you are equal to it.

An important exercise: while observing the mind in recitation, make every repetition of the Buddha's name prevail over deluded thoughts. At first, after reciting once, check whether it prevailed over deluded thoughts; once your practice has matured, you will know at the very moment of reciting whether it has prevailed. At this point, with every repetition, keep a clear awareness: has it prevailed over deluded thoughts? If not, find the cause and apply the right remedy. Practicing steadily in this way, over time your skill will ripen, and naturally your recitation will become one unbroken continuity, without dullness and without scattering. This exercise is extremely important: if the Buddha's name can prevail over deluded thoughts, it can prevail over birth and death. This is a matter on which your wisdom-life depends, and you must train hard.
[Practice becoming continuous] Reciting the Buddha's name without any admixture of deluded thoughts — the thought of recitation continues into one unbroken sheet.
Master Yinguang said:

“If your recitation cannot become pure and single, you must restrain the mind and not let it run outward; after a long while it will naturally become pure and single. ‘Becoming continuous’ means pure and single, without admixture.”
(From Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,
Fourth Letter in Reply to Layman Ma Qixi) Master Hanshan said:
“You must take this one sound of the Buddha's name
(the Buddha's name)
and bite down on it firmly,
resolved that it will prevail over deluded thoughts

. In all places, keep it present in every thought, and do not let it be veiled or obstructed by deluded thoughts. Applying such bitter and earnest effort, after a long while you will ripen in it, and naturally there will be a response — without seeking to become continuous, you will become continuous of itself.”
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
“Instructions to Layman Jingxin”)

Observing
the mind while reciting the Buddha's name

: in the initial stage, it is best to aim for the absence of deluded thoughts; then, one should take “aware the moment a deluded thought arises (the instant a deluded thought rises, immediately see it)” as the key point of practice. Once you achieve “aware the moment a deluded thought arises,” “aware, and it is gone” becomes very easy, and thereby you reach the point of not following deluded thoughts as they arise, and the state of single-mindedness without distraction becomes stable.
Aware the moment a deluded thought arises”

is an important skill in cultivating single-mindedness in recitation. Practice it constantly: while reciting, attend to the arising of deluded thoughts. Over time, you will be able to become aware the moment a deluded thought arises.

Deluded thoughts always arise at the gaps in your awareness. The practice of “aware the moment a deluded thought arises” is precisely the strengthening of awareness's continuity, mending these gaps. Therefore this practice must be made ever finer and denser.

There are many concrete methods for practicing “aware the moment a deluded thought arises.” For example, recite slowly, and after finishing one repetition, observe for a while before reciting the next; or while reciting, be aware of your own nature and see whether any deluded thought arises; and so on. Practice and experiment more, and you will find many good methods. Besides dedicated practice on the cushion, supplement it with practice off the cushion at any time and place, seizing every opportunity, and progress will be swift. With a correct method and hard training, success is certain. Therefore, for a practitioner who trains diligently, the most important thing is to find the practice method best suited to oneself (recognizing the way ahead).
An ancient worthy said:
“In cultivation there is nothing else to cultivate; one need only recognize the way ahead
(it lies solely in finding the practice method suited to oneself)
; once the way ahead is recognized
(once you have found the practice method suited to yourself)
, birth and death both come to rest.”

In truth, carefully observing and studying how deluded thoughts arise and how they envelop you so that you cannot break free is quite interesting. Even more interesting is that the more deeply you observe and study, the less easily deluded thoughts arise, and your practice advances swiftly. For example, you may be reciting well, your mind clear and still, when suddenly some disagreeable thoughts keep arising and cannot be dispelled. What then? Calm your mind and carefully observe and study how deluded thoughts arise and how they envelop you so that you cannot break free. Recite one repetition of the Buddha's name, then observe and study for a while; recite one repetition, then observe and study for a while. This is a wonderful method for shaking off deluded thoughts, and in the course of shaking them off your power grows rapidly — you really must thank these “sparring partners”!

Long ago, a monk went alone to a deep mountain to practice. At night he saw a fierce ghost rushing toward him. In his peril he hastened to recite the Buddha's name, and the ghost retreated again and again. But the moment the recitation stopped, the ghost pressed forward once more, so he had to recite without cease, all through the night, until daybreak when the ghost finally left. The same thing happened night after night. So the monk
simply

slept during the day and recited the Buddha's name all night long. In this way the stalemate continued year after year. In the end he attained the samādhi of Buddha-recitation, and the fierce ghost vanished without a trace. He was truly grateful to that ghost. (Commentary: this monk could perfectly well have moved to a place with no ghost, yet he advanced against the difficulty! This is the true character of a practitioner.)

In fact, every reciter of the Buddha's name likewise faces a fierce ghost — deluded thoughts. It lies in wait day and night, seeking to devour our wisdom-life of the Dharma body. So we must remain highly vigilant and beat back its every assault in time. In the end there are only two outcomes: either you subdue it, accomplish your practice, and are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; or it subdues you, leaving you to keep revolving through the six paths.

Observing the mind while reciting is extremely important; you must persist with unyielding perseverance, for where utmost sincerity reaches, even metal and stone give way. Recite until “the present thought is the Buddha-thought, and the Buddha-thought is the present thought,” and you will enter single-mindedness without distraction.
Master Zhongfeng taught:
The ancients' faith was pure and whole, their right causes awe-inspiring; they took birth and death to heart and pondered intently the revolving of transmigration
(earnestly reflecting on the dreadfulness of the six paths' revolving)
, so that the myriad conditions were laid to rest and pared away
(qinxiao: to stop, to cut away)
, and the hundred cares melted like ice. Raising a single sound of the Buddha's name, directly below there was no other view
(the Buddha-thought is the present thought, the present thought is the Buddha-thought)
Now then
(an introductory particle),

the thought that is Buddha is like the Tai'e sword, held horizontally across the courtyard; the Buddha that is the thought is like a great wheel of fire, its flames leaping to the stars. Whatever of the myriad things brushes against it is scorched; whatever touches it is wounded. Recite in this way for long, and besides the thought there is no other Buddha, besides the Buddha no other thought, body and mind in one accord
(mind and mouth in one accord)

, with the subject and object both forgotten. Talk of its arriving home admits of no sound; the words of a shortcut are not worth mentioning. It may be called a divine art for realizing the practice, surpassing expedients
(super-expedient)
, a true path, the thunder that shatters the sealed door of birth and death, the sun and moon that illumine the dark lanes of delusion.”
(Zhongfeng's Rite of the Threefold Remembrance)

[Besides the thought there is no other Buddha; besides the Buddha no other thought] The present thought is precisely the thought of reciting the Buddha's name, and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is precisely the present thought.

The skill of observing the mind while reciting is extremely important; practice it on and off the cushion again and again, with eyes open and eyes closed, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in different surroundings, and before falling asleep. You must be sure that the Buddha's name prevails over deluded thoughts and that you are not manipulated by them. Practice constantly amid circumstances, and test yourself amid circumstances. When your practice deepens, it is as Master Zhongfeng said:

“Besides the thought there is no other Buddha, besides the Buddha no other thought, body and mind in one accord, with subject and object both forgotten. Talk of its arriving home admits of no sound; the words of a shortcut are not worth mentioning. It may be called a divine art for realizing the practice, a true path surpassing expedients, the thunder that shatters the sealed door of birth and death, the sun and moon that illumine the dark lanes of delusion.”
Master Yinguang said:
“It is only that you will not return; return, and it is yours — who would contend with you for the wind and moonlight of your native home?”
Only now does one begin to grasp the wonder of the three words “return, and it is yours.”
It is only that you will not return; return, and it is yours
] The full couplet reads:

“You should make the vow, vow to be reborn there; let others cling to the streams and hills of the road of a sojourner. It is only that you will not return; return, and it is yours — who would contend with you for the wind and moonlight of your native home?”
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Preface to the Publication of the Collection on Longing to Return)
Question: Is there any contradiction between observing the mind and reciting the Buddha's name?
Answer: Not only is there no contradiction, they enhance one another. Master Yinguang said:

“When one first sets the mind on reciting the Buddha's name, before reaching the personal realization of samādhi, who can be entirely free of deluded thoughts? What matters is that the mind constantly stays aware and illumines, and does not follow delusions as they turn.”
(The Essence of Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,

“Instructions on Methods of Practice”) Here, “the mind constantly stays aware and illumines, and does not follow delusions as they turn” is precisely observing the mind. To recite the Buddha's name with this skill of observing the mind is like a tiger with horns — just try it yourself and you will know.
Question: Then why did Master Yinguang say:
“Do not use the method of observing the mind while reciting; use the method of gathering the mind while reciting.”
(Letter in Reply to Layman Yang Weizhang)

Answer: Because the other party (Layman Yang Weizhang) was a beginner without an adequate foundation, yet went ahead and used observing-the-mind recitation, causing his heart-fire to flare upward; for this reason he wrote to Master Yinguang for guidance. So in this letter Master Yinguang was prescribing medicine according to the other party's specific condition — not denying observing-the-mind recitation. Master Yinguang wrote:
“As an ordinary being of extremely heavy karmic obstructions,
you rashly used
the method of observing the mind,
and so brought about this result
(namely the ‘heart-fire flaring upward’ spoken of in the other's letter)
And he went on to write:
“The method of observing the mind is a method of the doctrinal schools for cultivating contemplation; it does not suit the disposition of those who recite the Buddha's name very well.”

Here, “does not suit the disposition of those who recite the Buddha's name very well” is a tactful way of saying that your foundation is not yet adequate for observing-the-mind recitation, which is why the heart-fire flared upward. Therefore,
Master Yinguang told him:
“Do not use the method of observing the mind while reciting; use the method of gathering the mind while reciting.”
In the Record of Groping for the Elephant of the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, Master Yinguang taught:
“As for the method,
you must,
at the very moment of reciting the Buddha's name,
turn your contemplation back upon the recitation itself
, concentrate on the single object, do not let the mind run outward, in every thought tend the source of the mind, and in every thought unite with the Buddha's essence.”
Is not the
“turn your contemplation back upon the recitation itself”

in this teaching precisely observing-the-mind recitation? Therefore Master Yinguang by no means opposed observing-the-mind recitation; he was speaking of whether it suited the person's disposition. Because beginners lack an adequate foundation, if they practice observing-the-mind recitation they will often experience dizziness, headache, heart-fire flaring upward, and the like, so it is not advisable for them.

Therefore, wonderful as observing-the-mind recitation is, it does not suit those whose foundation is insufficient. It is advisable to first practice investigative recitation, and only begin observing-the-mind recitation after laying a solid foundation.
Observing the mind while reciting is the essence of reciting the Buddha's name; since ancient times many patriarchs and great masters have attained single-mindedness without distraction through it.
